1.q: What is Python, in one line?
1.a: An easy-to-read, general-purpose language made by Guido van Rossum in 1991. It is named after the comedy show Monty Python, not the snake.
1.hook: Python: write the idea, not the ceremony.

1.q: Why does Python use indentation instead of { } and ;?
1.a: Python was made so code is easy for humans to read. Blocks are shown by indentation (4 spaces by PEP 8), so the code looks like neat notes. Java needs a class and a main method just to print; Python needs one line.

1.q: What happens when you run `python hello.py`? (3 steps)
1.a: 1. Python checks the grammar of the WHOLE file (SyntaxError here, nothing runs). 2. It converts the code into bytecode: small step cards. 3. The Python Virtual Machine (PVM) carries out the cards one by one (NameError, TypeError and other runtime errors happen here).
1.hook: Grammar is checked before cooking; missing ingredients are found while cooking.

1.q: A file has two `print()` lines, then line 3 is `x = = 5`. What prints?
1.a: Nothing. You only get `SyntaxError: invalid syntax`, because Python checks the whole file before running any line.

1.q: A file has two `print()` lines, then line 3 uses a name that doesn't exist. What prints?
1.a: Both print lines run, then `NameError`. Runtime errors only appear when Python reaches that line.
1.out:
line 1
line 2
NameError: name 'saffron' is not defined

1.q: What is bytecode?
1.a: The simple step-by-step instructions Python makes from your code, like "load a, load b, add". The CPU can't run it directly; the PVM does. You can see it with `dis.dis(function)`.

1.q: What are `.pyc` files and the `__pycache__` folder?
1.a: Saved bytecode, so Python can skip converting the code again next time. Python saves them only for modules you import, not for the script you run directly.

1.q: Does the PVM turn bytecode into machine code?
1.a: No. The PVM is a C program that is already machine code. It reads each bytecode instruction and does it directly: the cook follows the card, it doesn't rewrite it. Turning bytecode into machine code is what a JIT does (PyPy, and CPython's experimental JIT).
1.hook: The cook follows the card; a JIT rewrites the card.

1.q: Is Python compiled or interpreted?
1.a: Both. CPython compiles the code to bytecode, then the PVM interprets that bytecode. It is called interpreted because you never run a separate compile step and you never get an .exe.
1.hook: Interview line: "Usually called interpreted, but technically it's compiled to bytecode and then interpreted."

1.q: What is CPython? Does your Python code go through a C compiler?
1.a: CPython is the normal Python you download: the interpreter program, written in C. Your Python code never goes through a C compiler; it is turned into bytecode and run by the PVM.

1.q: Name other versions (implementations) of Python.
1.a: PyPy (has a JIT, pure-Python loops often run much faster), MicroPython (small microcontroller boards), Jython (runs on Java's JVM), IronPython (runs on .NET).

1.q: What is the latest Python version, and what's new?
1.a: 3.15, released October 2026: lazy imports (`lazy import json`), a built-in `frozendict`, UTF-8 as the default encoding, a faster experimental JIT. In 3.14 the free-threaded build (no GIL) became officially supported. Python 2 was retired in 2020.

1.q: Python 2 vs Python 3: three differences?
1.a: 1. `print "hi"` became `print("hi")`. 2. `5 / 2` gave 2, now gives 2.5 (use `//` for 2). 3. Text is Unicode by default in Python 3.

1.q: "Everything is an object": what does that mean?
1.a: Every value (5, "hi", a list, even a function) is a box in memory with a value, a type (`type(x)`) and an identity (`id(x)`, its address in CPython). Even a function can get a new label.

1.q: What is a variable in Python?
1.a: A label (name) stuck on an object, not a box that holds the value. Two labels can point to the same object.

1.q: What does dynamically typed mean?
1.a: The type belongs to the object, not the variable. A label can move to an object of another type, and types are checked while the program runs. So you never write `int x`.

1.q: What does strongly typed mean? Can Python mix types at all?
1.a: Python never silently guesses between unrelated types: `"1" + 1` is a TypeError. Mixes that make sense are allowed.
1.out:
5.5 2 ababab
TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str
1.hook: Labels can move (dynamic); apples and oranges never mix (strong).

1.q: Dynamic vs static, strong vs weak: where do Python, JavaScript, Java and C sit?
1.a: Python: dynamic + strong. JavaScript: dynamic + weak (`"1" + 1` gives "11"). Java: static + strong. C: static + weak. Dynamic does NOT mean weak.

1.q: How does Python free memory?
1.a: It counts the labels (references) on each object; when the count reaches zero, the object is deleted. A garbage collector also cleans up groups of objects that only point at each other. You never free memory yourself.
1.hook: Count the labels; zero labels = thrown away.

1.q: Why is Python slower than C or Rust?
1.a: On every operation, like `a + b`, Python checks the types again because labels may have moved, and the PVM reads instructions one by one. C checks types once, before running.
1.hook: Python checks every time; C checks once.

1.q: What is the GIL, in simple words?
1.a: In standard CPython only one thread runs Python code at a time: one knife in the kitchen. Fine for waiting jobs (downloads, API calls), no speed-up for heavy CPU work. Since 3.14 there is an official free-threaded build without it.

1.q: If Python is slow, why is AI built in it?
1.a: Python is the manager; the heavy maths runs in C, C++ or CUDA inside libraries like NumPy and PyTorch. Measured: adding 10 million numbers took ~0.46 s with a Python loop and ~0.007 s with NumPy (~65x). Your Zen-harness: Python logic, llama.cpp (C++) does the model maths.
1.hook: A slow manager doesn't matter when fast workers do 99% of the work.

1.q: Main reasons to choose Python?
1.a: Fast to write and read, a library for almost everything (NumPy, pandas, PyTorch, FastAPI), a great glue layer over C/C++/Rust, a huge community. Ideal for rapid prototyping and AI.

1.q: Limitations of Python?
1.a: Slow pure-Python loops, the GIL for CPU-heavy threads, more memory per value, weak for mobile and browser apps, and type mistakes only show up when that line runs.

1.q: Where is Python used?
1.a: AI/ML (PyTorch, scikit-learn), data (pandas, Jupyter), web backends (Django, Flask, FastAPI), automation and scripting, testing (pytest), science (SciPy).

1.q: What are a PEP, PEP 8 and PEP 20?
1.a: PEP = Python Enhancement Proposal, the document for proposing changes. PEP 8 = the style guide (4 spaces, snake_case). PEP 20 = the Zen of Python: `import this` shows 19 rules, starting "Beautiful is better than ugly."

1.q: Is Python object-oriented or functional?
1.a: Multi-paradigm: you can write procedural code, object-oriented code (classes) and functional code (lambda, map, filter).

1.q: Is Python case-sensitive?
1.a: Yes: `name` and `Name` are different variables, and `True`, `False`, `None` must start with a capital letter.

1.q: REPL vs script: what is the difference in output?
1.a: The REPL (`python`, the >>> prompt) shows the value of each expression automatically. A script shows only what you `print()`. A script containing only `2 + 3` prints nothing.

1.q: What does `python -m` do, and why `python -m pip`?
1.a: It runs a module as a program: `python -m venv .venv`, `python -m json.tool file.json`, `python -m http.server`. `python -m pip` installs into the Python you are running; plain `pip` might belong to another installed version.

1.q: Name the indentation errors.
1.a: No indent after a `:` line: IndentationError "expected an indented block". Uneven dedent: IndentationError "unindent does not match any outer indentation level". Mixing tabs and spaces: TabError. For an empty block, write `pass`.

1.q: Comment vs docstring?
1.a: A `#` comment is ignored completely and explains why. A docstring is the first string inside a function, class or module; it is stored in `__doc__`, shown by `help()`, and explains what the code does and how to use it. A loose triple-quoted string in the middle of code is not a real comment: it is a string created and thrown away.
1.code:
def greet(name):
    """Return a greeting for name."""
    return "Hello " + name
print(greet.__doc__)

1.q: Variable naming rules and PEP 8 style?
1.a: Letters, digits and `_`; cannot start with a digit; case-sensitive; cannot be a keyword. Valid: `_x`, `user2`, `Class`. Invalid: `2x`, `my-var`, `class`. Style: snake_case for variables and functions, PascalCase for classes, UPPER_CASE for constants.

1.q: What goes wrong here?
1.a: You hid the built-in `list`, so it is no longer callable. Never name variables after built-ins.

1.q: What does `print(print("hi"))` show? And `sep` / `end`?
1.a: `hi`, then `None`, because `print()` itself returns None. `sep` sets what goes between values, `end` what goes at the end (default newline).
1.code:
print(print("hi"))
print("a", "b", sep="-")
print("x", end=" | ")
print("y")

1.q: What type does `input()` return?
1.a: Always a string. Convert it yourself: `int(input("Age: "))`. Converting text that isn't a whole number raises ValueError.
1.code:
s = "5"  # what input() would give
print(s * 2, int(s) * 2)
int("3.5")
1.out:
55 10
ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '3.5'

1.q: How many keywords does Python have? Is `print` one?
1.a: 35 (`import keyword; keyword.kwlist`). `True`, `False`, `None` are keywords; `print` is not, it is a function. Soft keywords act as keywords only in some places: `match`, `case`, `_`, `type`, and `lazy` (new in 3.15), so `match = 5` still works.

1.q: What is `None`, and how do you check for it?
1.a: The one "no value" object (type NoneType). A function without `return` gives None. It counts as false, and `None == 0` is False. Check with `x is None`, not `x == None`.

1.q: Swap two variables in one line?
1.a: `a, b = b, a`. Also `x = y = 0` sets both to 0.
1.code:
a, b = 1, 2
a, b = b, a
print(a, b)

70.q: Why Rust for zen but Python for Zen-harness?
70.a: Measured on my machine: the Python prototype took ~12 s per reply, the Rust version ~3 s, with the same models. zen handles audio every 20 ms and must stop instantly when interrupted, so it needs a fast manager with real parallelism and no GIL in callbacks, shipped as one .exe. Zen-harness mostly waits seconds for the model, so Python's ecosystem wins.
70.hook: Pick the language for the bottleneck: milliseconds -> Rust, model time -> Python.

70.q: Interviewer: "The models are C++ either way. Why was Python 4x slower?"
70.a: The gain came from orchestration, not raw speed: in zen the stages stream and overlap (speech starts with the first ~250 ms audio chunk), C callbacks never wait for a GIL, and the models stay loaded. Check which of these was true for your Python prototype before you say it.

70.q: Rust reason 1: the C libraries call back into your code.
70.a: The TTS DLL calls Rust with every audio chunk (~250 ms) and checks a Rust cancel flag between chunks (`tts.rs`). In Python, every callback from C must grab the GIL first, so it can wait. Callbacks are wrapped in `catch_unwind`, and the native libraries run in separate worker processes.

70.q: Rust reason 2: many jobs at once, safely.
70.a: Capture every 20 ms, voice detection, transcription on its own thread, LLM streaming, speech streaming, all cancellable at once. Rust runs them truly in parallel (tokio + threads), and data races are compile errors. Python's asyncio is one thread, and Python never checks for races at compile time, even without the GIL.

70.q: Rust reason 3: wrong states can't be written.
70.a: Every background job carries the generation number of its turn, so a stale reply after an interruption is dropped, never spoken (`session.rs`). An LLM slot ID outside 0-1 can't even be created (`engine.rs`). About 300 Rust tests.
Slower to write, long optimised builds, a smaller ML ecosystem. That's why Zen-harness is Python. Saying the trade-off out loud makes the choice sound deliberate.

FFI: one language calling functions written in another (Rust calling the C/C++ speech libraries). Data race: two threads use the same data at the same time and at least one of them writes; Rust refuses to compile that.
